title: How Long After Antibiotics Can You Drink? Drug-by-Drug Wait Times
excerpt: How long to wait after antibiotics before drinking, drug by drug: the 72-hour rule for metronidazole and tinidazole, which antibiotics need no wait, and when to ask.
metaDescription: How long after antibiotics can you drink? Drug-by-drug wait times, the 72-hour rule for Flagyl and tinidazole, and which antibiotics need no wait at all.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** for most common antibiotics, there's no official waiting period at all. Amoxicillin, cephalexin, azithromycin, doxycycline, ciprofloxacin, and nitrofurantoin don't have a dangerous chemical reaction with a moderate amount of alcohol, so you don't need to count hours after your last pill. The real exceptions are **metronidazole (Flagyl)** and **tinidazole (Tindamax)**, where the label says to wait **at least 72 hours (three full days)** after your last dose, plus a few hospital and specialist drugs with their own rules. For everything else, the more useful question isn't "how many hours" but "am I actually better yet?"

**The quick rules:** Find your antibiotic in the wait table below. If it's metronidazole or tinidazole, wait three full days after the last dose. If it's a hospital IV antibiotic you don't know the name of, ask before your first drink. If it's linezolid or a tuberculosis drug, follow the specific advice from your prescriber. For the rest, there's no required gap, but waiting until you've finished the course and your symptoms have cleared is the sensible choice, and a 24 to 48 hour buffer after the last dose costs you very little.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who prescribed your antibiotic and knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking if** you're not sure which antibiotic you took, you got antibiotics through an IV in hospital, you take other medicines, you have liver or kidney disease, or your infection was serious. **Get medical help right away if** you develop trouble breathing, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, chest pain, fainting, a severe headache, or vomiting you can't stop after drinking. In an emergency, call 911.

## Why the Waiting Period Depends on the Drug: The Real Mechanism

"How long after antibiotics can you drink" has a different answer for different drugs because antibiotics clash with alcohol in different ways, and some don't clash at all. There are two things that decide how long you should wait.

### 1. Whether the drug actually reacts with alcohol

When you drink, your liver turns alcohol into **acetaldehyde**, a toxic compound that contributes to that sick, flushed feeling after heavy drinking. A second enzyme, **aldehyde dehydrogenase**, then turns acetaldehyde into harmless acetate.

A few antibiotics have been linked to interfering with this clean-up step, so acetaldehyde can build up. Doctors call this a **disulfiram-like reaction**, named after disulfiram (Antabuse), a medicine that blocks the same step on purpose. The symptoms are flushing, a pounding headache, nausea and vomiting, a racing heart, and sometimes dizziness or a drop in blood pressure. This is why the strict waiting periods exist.

How strong and how common this reaction really is with metronidazole has been debated by researchers (more on that below), but the label warning stands and the reaction isn't worth testing on yourself.

Most antibiotics don't touch this pathway at all. For them, there's no reaction to wait out.

### 2. How long the drug stays in your body

Every drug has a **half-life**, which is how long it takes your body to clear half of it. After about five half-lives, almost all of the drug is gone. For drugs that do react with alcohol, the waiting period is built to cover that clearing time with a safety margin on top.

That's where the 72-hour rule for metronidazole comes from. Metronidazole's half-life is roughly 8 hours, so most of it is gone within about two days. The extra day is a buffer, partly because the enzyme effects may take time to settle and partly because clearance is slower in some people, such as those with liver problems.

Half-life also explains why "how long does the antibiotic stay in my system" doesn't matter much for drugs with no alcohol interaction. Azithromycin, for example, lingers in the body for days after a Z-Pak, but because it doesn't react with alcohol, that long tail doesn't create a waiting period.

## How Long After Antibiotics Can You Drink? Drug-by-Drug Wait Table

This is general label and reference guidance for healthy adults, not a substitute for your own prescription label. "No required wait" means there's no known dangerous reaction, not that drinking is a good idea while you're still sick.

| Antibiotic (common brand) | Wait after last dose | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Metronidazole (Flagyl) | At least 72 hours | Label warns of a disulfiram-like reaction |
| Tinidazole (Tindamax) | At least 72 hours | Same drug family, same label warning |
| Secnidazole (Solosec) | Ask your pharmacist | Same drug family; single-dose product |
| Cefotetan, cefoperazone (hospital IV) | About 72 hours | Disulfiram-like reaction reported |
| Linezolid (Zyvox) | Ask your prescriber, especially about tap beer and red wine | Tyramine interaction, not acetaldehyde |
| Isoniazid, rifampin (tuberculosis) | Follow your clinic's advice | Added liver strain with daily drinking |
| Sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim (Bactrim, Septra) | No formal wait; many people wait a day or two | Occasional reaction reports; shared side effects |
| Doxycycline (Vibramycin, Doryx) | No required wait | Heavy drinking may lower drug levels during the course |
| Amoxicillin, penicillin | No required wait | No significant direct interaction |
| Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Augmentin) | No required wait | Alcohol may worsen stomach upset |
| Azithromycin (Zithromax, Z-Pak) | No required wait | No significant direct interaction |
| Cephalexin (Keflex), cefdinir, cefuroxime | No required wait | No significant direct interaction |
| Ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin | No required wait; go easy if dizzy | Dizziness and fogginess can stack |
| Nitrofurantoin (Macrobid) | No required wait | Alcohol may add to nausea |
| Clindamycin (Cleocin) | No required wait | Alcohol may worsen stomach upset and diarrhea |

For a fuller look at how each of these behaves while you're still taking it, see our main guide to [antibiotics and alcohol](/never-hungover/antibiotics-and-alcohol).

## How Long After Metronidazole (Flagyl) Can You Drink?

**Wait at least 72 hours after your last dose.** This is the antibiotic where the waiting period really matters, and it's the one most people are searching about.

The US label for metronidazole warns against drinking during treatment and for at least three days afterward because of the risk of abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, headache, and flushing. That applies whether you took a week-long course or a single large dose, such as the one-time dose sometimes used for trichomoniasis. A single dose doesn't clear any faster just because it was one pill.

### Is the reaction as bad as people say?

The science here is messier than the warning suggests. A review in *Annals of Pharmacotherapy* in 2000 looked at the published reports and concluded that the evidence for a true disulfiram-like reaction with metronidazole was weaker than commonly believed, and that many reported cases had other explanations. Some small studies haven't been able to reproduce the reaction reliably.

That doesn't make drinking safe. Case reports of real reactions exist, the label warning hasn't changed, and there's no way to know in advance whether you'll react. Treat the 72 hours as a firm rule. If you've already slipped up, our guide on [what to do if you accidentally drank on metronidazole](/never-hungover/accidentally-drank-on-metronidazole) walks through it calmly, and our full [metronidazole and alcohol](/never-hungover/metronidazole-and-alcohol) guide covers the details.

### Hidden alcohol during the 72 hours

The waiting period covers all alcohol, not just drinks. During the course and the three days after, watch for:

- **Mouthwash** with alcohol (switch to an alcohol-free one)
- **Liquid cough and cold medicines** that list alcohol as an ingredient (we cover alternatives in our [alcohol-free cold medicine](/never-hungover/alcohol-free-cold-medicine) guide)
- **Kombucha**, which naturally contains a little alcohol
- **Food cooked with wine or spirits** added late in cooking
- **"Non-alcoholic" beer and wine**, which can still contain up to about 0.5% alcohol

## How Long After Tinidazole Can You Drink?

**Wait at least 72 hours after your last dose.** Tinidazole (Tindamax) is a close chemical cousin of metronidazole used for many of the same infections, including bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, and giardia. Its label carries the same kind of warning: no alcohol during treatment and for three days afterward. Tinidazole stays in the body a bit longer than metronidazole, so don't shave time off the three days.

**Secnidazole** (Solosec), a newer single-dose drug in the same family, is less clear-cut in public guidance. Because it shares the same chemical structure, the cautious approach is to ask your pharmacist how long to avoid alcohol around your dose rather than guessing.

## How Long After Amoxicillin Can You Drink?

**There's no required waiting period.** Amoxicillin doesn't have a known meaningful interaction with alcohol, and it leaves the body quickly (its half-life is about an hour). Once you've finished the course, you can drink as you normally would from a drug standpoint.

The same goes for plain penicillin and for **Augmentin** (amoxicillin with clavulanate), with one practical note: Augmentin commonly causes stomach upset and diarrhea, and alcohol can make both worse. If your stomach is still unsettled after the course, give it a day or two. Our [amoxicillin and alcohol](/never-hungover/amoxicillin-and-alcohol) page goes into more detail.

## How Long After Azithromycin (Z-Pak) Can You Drink?

**There's no required waiting period.** This one confuses people because azithromycin stays in your body for a long time. Its half-life is roughly 68 hours, which is why a five-day Z-Pak keeps working for several days after the last tablet. But a long half-life only matters if the drug reacts with alcohol, and azithromycin doesn't have a known significant interaction.

So the practical answer is: you don't need to wait out the drug, but if you're still coughing or feeling run down, wait until you're properly recovered. See our [azithromycin and alcohol](/never-hungover/azithromycin-and-alcohol) guide for more.

## How Long After Doxycycline Can You Drink?

**There's no required waiting period after you finish.** The doxycycline issue is about *during* the course, not after. The label notes that chronic heavy drinking can speed up how fast the liver clears doxycycline, which may lower its levels in your blood. That's a concern with regular heavy drinking, not a drink or two, and it stops being relevant once you've finished the prescription.

Doxycycline can also irritate the throat and stomach, and alcohol doesn't help with that. If you're taking it for a long stretch, such as for acne or malaria prevention, ask your prescriber what's reasonable. More in our [doxycycline and alcohol](/never-hungover/doxycycline-and-alcohol) guide.

## How Long After Ciprofloxacin Can You Drink?

**There's no required waiting period.** Ciprofloxacin (Cipro) and levofloxacin don't have a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol. They can cause dizziness, lightheadedness, and occasionally confusion or mood changes, and alcohol can add to those effects. If you've had any of those side effects, wait until they've fully cleared before drinking. Cipro's half-life is around four hours, so the drug itself is mostly gone within a day of your last dose. Our [ciprofloxacin and alcohol](/never-hungover/ciprofloxacin-and-alcohol) page has the details.

## How Long After Bactrim Can You Drink?

**There's no official waiting period, but a short buffer is reasonable.** Sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim (Bactrim, Septra) has scattered case reports of disulfiram-like reactions with alcohol, though the link is much less established than with metronidazole. Both of its components have half-lives of roughly 8 to 11 hours, so most of the drug is gone within two to three days of the last dose. Many pharmacists suggest waiting a day or two after finishing. If you had nausea or a rash on Bactrim, check with your prescriber first. See our [Bactrim and alcohol](/never-hungover/bactrim-and-alcohol) guide.

## How Long After Cephalexin (Keflex) Can You Drink?

**There's no required waiting period** for cephalexin and the other cephalosporins you'd typically get from a family doctor or urgent care, such as cefdinir, cefuroxime, and cefadroxil. Cephalexin clears quickly, with a half-life of about an hour.

The exception is a small group of cephalosporins, such as **cefotetan** and **cefoperazone**, that contain a chemical side group linked to disulfiram-like reactions. These are almost always given by IV in hospital. If that's you, avoid alcohol during treatment and for about three days after. More in our [cephalexin and alcohol](/never-hungover/cephalexin-and-alcohol) guide.

## After IV Antibiotics or a Hospital Stay

If you received antibiotics through a drip in hospital and you're not sure which ones, **ask before your first drink.** Hospital treatment is where you're most likely to meet the drugs with real alcohol warnings: IV metronidazole, cefotetan, and linezolid among them. Your discharge paperwork usually lists the medicines you were given, or the pharmacist at the hospital can tell you. A hospital stay also usually means a more serious infection, so recovery time matters even if the drug itself has no interaction.

## Linezolid and Tuberculosis Drugs: Special Cases

**Linezolid (Zyvox)** is used for serious infections, including some resistant ones. Its issue with alcohol is different. Linezolid weakly blocks an enzyme called monoamine oxidase, which also breaks down **tyramine**, a substance found in aged and fermented foods and some drinks. Tyramine buildup can cause a sudden, dangerous rise in blood pressure. Tap and draft beer, unpasteurized beers, and some red wines can be high in tyramine. Ask your prescriber how long to avoid these after your course, and get emergency help for a sudden severe headache, chest pain, or a pounding heartbeat.

**Tuberculosis drugs** such as isoniazid and rifampin are taken for months, and isoniazid in particular can injure the liver. Daily alcohol use raises that risk. TB clinics generally advise avoiding alcohol during treatment, and they may check your liver enzymes. Ask them when it's safe to drink again.

## What About Antifungals?

People often lump antifungals in with antibiotics, and two are worth a mention. **Fluconazole** (Diflucan), the common yeast infection pill, has no well-established reaction with alcohol, though both are processed by the liver. Our [fluconazole and alcohol](/never-hungover/fluconazole-and-alcohol) guide covers it. **Griseofulvin**, an older antifungal used for scalp and nail infections, carries a label warning that it can intensify the effects of alcohol, causing a racing heart and flushing. If you take griseofulvin, ask your pharmacist how long to wait after your course.

## Can You Drink the Same Day You Finish Antibiotics?

For drugs with no interaction, such as amoxicillin, cephalexin, or azithromycin, having a drink on the evening of your last dose isn't known to be dangerous. Whether it's wise is another matter. Many people finish their course on the day their symptoms are just starting to fade, and alcohol can make that last stretch of recovery slower.

For metronidazole and tinidazole, **no.** The clock starts at your last pill and runs for 72 hours.

## Is 24 or 48 Hours Enough?

For metronidazole and tinidazole, **no.** Neither 24 nor 48 hours meets the label's three-day window.

For drugs without a known alcohol reaction, there's no required wait, so 24 to 48 hours is more than enough from a drug standpoint. A day or two of buffer can still make sense if your stomach is still upset or you still feel tired, since alcohol makes both worse.

## Why Waiting Until You Feel Better Still Matters

Even when the drug clears and there's no interaction, there are good reasons not to rush back to drinking:

- **Your immune system is still finishing the job.** Heavy drinking can temporarily weaken parts of the immune response. A night of heavy drinking right after an infection isn't ideal timing.
- **Sleep matters for recovery, and alcohol disrupts it.** Alcohol can help you fall asleep but tends to fragment sleep later in the night.
- **Dehydration and stomach upset stack.** Many antibiotics leave the gut unsettled for a few days, and alcohol irritates the stomach and adds to dehydration.
- **You might mistake side effects for a hangover, or a hangover for a relapse.** Feeling rough the morning after can make it hard to tell whether your infection is coming back.

A common worry is whether drinking "undoes" the antibiotic. For most drugs, a moderate amount of alcohol doesn't stop the antibiotic from working. We cover that in detail in [does alcohol make antibiotics less effective](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-make-antibiotics-less-effective).

## Don't Stop Your Antibiotics Early to Drink Sooner

This is the mistake worth avoiding most. Stopping a course early so you can drink at a wedding or a weekend event can leave an infection only partly treated, which can mean it comes back. If you have an event coming up and you're on metronidazole or tinidazole, talk to your prescriber. Sometimes a different antibiotic is an option, but that's their call to make, not yours.

And if you're on one of the drugs with no interaction, you don't need to stop at all. A drink or two is generally considered low risk, even if skipping alcohol until you're better is the kinder choice.

## When to See a Doctor

Contact your doctor or pharmacist, or get urgent care, if after drinking on or soon after antibiotics you have:

- Flushing with a pounding headache, racing heart, and vomiting (possible disulfiram-like reaction)
- A sudden, severe headache or chest pain (especially on linezolid)
- Trouble breathing, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or a widespread rash (possible allergic reaction, which can happen with antibiotics regardless of alcohol)
- Yellowing skin or eyes, dark urine, or pain under the right ribs (possible liver strain)
- Severe or bloody diarrhea, which can be a sign of a gut infection after antibiotics and needs medical attention whether or not you drank

If symptoms are severe, call 911.

## A Note on Supplements and Getting Back to Normal

Once you're cleared to drink again and feeling well, the usual habits matter most: eat beforehand, alternate with water, and pace yourself. Our guide on [how long alcohol stays in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system) explains how fast the body processes a drink, and [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the evidence-based basics.

Some people also use **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so think of it as promising rather than settled. It has no role in the antibiotic waiting period: there is no good evidence that DHM prevents a metronidazole reaction or changes how any antibiotic interacts with alcohol, so don't use it to shorten the 72 hours. It's also sensible to skip non-essential supplements during an antibiotic course unless your pharmacist says they're fine. If you want to try DHM later on a normal night out, options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing, and our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what to check if you take other medicines.

## The Bottom Line

- **Metronidazole and tinidazole:** wait at least 72 hours after your last dose, and watch for hidden alcohol.
- **Hospital IV cephalosporins like cefotetan:** about 72 hours; ask if you're not sure what you were given.
- **Linezolid and TB drugs:** follow your prescriber's specific advice.
- **Amoxicillin, azithromycin, cephalexin, doxycycline, ciprofloxacin, nitrofurantoin, clindamycin:** no required wait after you finish.
- **Bactrim:** no formal wait, but a day or two is a reasonable buffer.
- Whatever you took, wait until you feel recovered, and never cut a course short to drink sooner.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How long after antibiotics can you drink alcohol?**

It depends on the antibiotic. For metronidazole (Flagyl) and tinidazole (Tindamax), wait at least 72 hours after your last dose. For a few hospital and specialist drugs, such as cefotetan, linezolid, and tuberculosis medicines, follow your prescriber's advice. For most common antibiotics, including amoxicillin, azithromycin, cephalexin, doxycycline, and ciprofloxacin, there's no required waiting period, though it's sensible to wait until you've finished the course and feel better.

**How long after metronidazole can I drink?**

At least 72 hours (three full days) after your last dose. The label warns that alcohol during treatment or within three days of stopping can cause cramps, nausea, vomiting, headache, and flushing. This applies to single-dose treatment too. Avoid hidden alcohol in mouthwash and liquid medicines during that window as well.

**How long after amoxicillin can I drink alcohol?**

There's no required waiting period. Amoxicillin has no known significant interaction with alcohol and clears from the body quickly. If you took Augmentin and still have an upset stomach or diarrhea, give it a day or two, since alcohol can make those worse.

**Can I drink after finishing a Z-Pak?**

Yes, from a drug interaction standpoint. Azithromycin stays in the body for several days after the last tablet, but it doesn't have a known significant interaction with alcohol, so that long half-life doesn't create a waiting period. If you're still unwell, it's better to wait until you've recovered.

**Is 48 hours enough after metronidazole?**

No. The label advises at least 72 hours after the last dose. Drinking at 48 hours falls inside that window. Wait the full three days.

**Should I stop my antibiotics early so I can drink at an event?**

No. Stopping early can leave an infection only partly treated. If you're on an antibiotic with no alcohol interaction, you don't need to stop, and a drink or two is generally considered low risk. If you're on metronidazole or tinidazole and have an event coming up, talk to your prescriber about your options.

**What happens if I drink too soon after metronidazole?**

Some people feel nothing, while others get flushing, a throbbing headache, nausea, vomiting, and a racing heart. Stop drinking, sip water, and rest. Get medical help if symptoms are severe, you can't keep fluids down, you feel faint, or you have chest pain or trouble breathing.

**Does DHM help me drink sooner after antibiotics?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents a metronidazole-type reaction or changes how antibiotics interact with alcohol. Follow your antibiotic's waiting period regardless of any supplement, and check with your pharmacist before adding supplements during a course.
